articles.title: 'More harm than good': Burnham reopens Brexit question, puts EU rejoin back on the table
articles.summary: British prime minister Andy Burnham has reopened one of the country's most divisive political questions, saying Brexit has done \"more harm than good\" and
articles.body: British prime minister Andy Burnham has reopened one of the country's most divisive political questions, saying Brexit has done "more harm than good" and signalling that Britain could consider everything from a closer relationship with the European Union to eventually rejoining the bloc.Speaking at the Labour Party conference, Burnham said the UK's current relationship with Europe was not "good enough" and promised to set out different options around a UK-EU summit later this year. Asked directly whether Britain should rejoin the EU, he said he wanted to "look at the options", ranging from staying as it is to considering a customs union, the single market or going "all the way".The comments mark a significant shift from the position Labour took at the 2024 election, when it promised to "make Brexit work" while ruling out rejoining the EU's customs union or single market. Burnham had also previously said he did not want to "re-run" the Brexit argument.Why did Britain vote for Brexit?On June 23, 2016, Britain voted by 52% to 48% to leave the EU. Nine months later, Theresa May triggered Article 50, formally beginning the process of withdrawal.The decision was not driven by one issue alone. Research by Professor Paul Whiteley and colleagues, using more than a decade of survey data, found that attitudes towards EU membership were closely tied to whether voters felt it was delivering on issues including economic prosperity, control over immigration, public services, crime and terrorism.The 2008 financial crisis and its aftermath also shaped the political mood. The research found that Britain's slow recovery left sections of the electorate feeling economically dissatisfied and politically unrepresented.Immigration was another major factor. The refugee and migration flows that followed upheaval in the Middle East and North Africa, particularly after the Arab Spring, intensified concerns about whether Britain and the EU could control migration. The research found that immigration and perceptions of lost control hardened Eurosceptic attitudes.But Brexit was not simply a change in Britain's political relationship with Europe. It altered the economic framework through which Britain traded with its largest nearby market.The post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement removed tariffs on most goods trade but did not preserve the UK's previous access to the EU single market and customs union. British businesses now face customs procedures, rules-of-origin requirements and additional regulatory paperwork, while services companies lost some of the market access they had enjoyed as part of the EU. Free movement also ended.How did Brexit impact Britain?Trade has been one of the clearest areas of change.British firms trading with the EU have had to absorb additional paperwork and regulatory costs. The result has been a decline in the number of firms exporting to the EU even where overall trade figures appear relatively resilient.Services have proved more resilient, particularly Britain's high-value digital sectors, but regulated industries such as financial and legal services have faced new barriers because the post-Brexit agreement provides less access than single-market membership.Brexit also created uncertainty for companies that had previously used Britain as a base for accessing European markets. Lower investment matters because it affects the capital available to businesses and, ultimately, productivity.Immigration was at the heart of the Brexit debate, but the post-Brexit picture turned out to be more complicated than simply "less immigration".Leaving the EU ended free movement and sharply reduced EU migration. Industries including hospitality, agriculture, logistics, food processing and manufacturing lost access to a familiar pool of European workers. Businesses responded in different ways, including through higher prices, lower output and changes to their operating models.At the same time, non-EU migration increased through work and study routes. As a result, the overall migration story became one of composition rather than a straightforward fall in numbers.That is particularly relevant to Burnham's comments because he has framed Britain's future relationship with Europe partly around immigration and economic control. His conference speech said the current settlement had failed to provide sufficient control over either area.What does Burnham's statement mean?Burnham has not announced that Britain will rejoin the EU but is reconsidering a position Labour had previously rejected.He said Britain could remain where it is, consider a customs union, consider the single market or "go all the way" back into the EU, while stressing that the options would need to be examined for what is actually doable and what their pros and cons would be.The immediate agenda is more modest; Burnham has already pointed to closer cooperation with Europe on immigration and measures to help British industries affected by Brexit. He plans to use the delayed UK-EU summit later this year to lay out longer-term options and seek consensus around one of them.Labour's previous approach was essentially to accept Brexit and make the existing settlement work better. Burnham is now questioning whether the settlement itself is good enough.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: In 2023, Steven Cohen paid $19.2 million for a Nantucket mansion; he then sought approval to demolish the six-bedroom main house
articles.summary: A lawyer's recent $19.2 million purchase of a Nantucket mansion, initially built in 2022, is facing scrutiny as he seeks to demolish the newly constructed home. Neighbors voice concerns over recurring teardowns in the area, raising questions about sustainability and neighborhood integrity.
articles.body: A newly constructed waterfront mansion on Nantucket could be headed for the wrecking ball soon after it changed hands. Sold for $19.2 million in November 2023, the home became the subject of a demolition proposal in 2024, according to the NY Post. Steven Cohen, identified as the buyer by NY Post, became the owner of the six-bedroom home through a blind trust in November 2023.According to Nantucket Current, Cohen filed a proposal with the Nantucket Historic District Commission (HDC), requesting permission to raze the multi-million-dollar residence.The request was scheduled for an official commission hearing and drew scrutiny from a local resident. Despite its high-end architectural design, the proposal outlines plans to demolish the estate in its entirety. The owner intends to replace the property's current footprint with a smaller one, consisting of a new 3,426-square-foot primary residence alongside a 528-square-foot detached guest house.The plan to swap size for a complete overhaul Initially completed in 2022 following a collaborative effort that involved several designers and builders, the property consists of a main house decked with six bedrooms and a two-bedroom guest house, offering eight bedrooms in total. Previously listed on the market by J Pepper Frazier Real Estate, the property includes several luxury amenities It features a swimming pool, a pickleball court, direct beach access, and sweeping views across Nantucket Harbor.Although the home's high-end finishes and natural stone accents were elucidated in the promotional listing, the interior of the structure actually remained incomplete, as the owner's representative testimony revealed to the HDC in July. Representing the property owner, architect Matthew MacEachern of the island-based design firm Emeritus made clear the physical condition of the residence during initial structural reviews before the HDC.According to MacEachern, the mansion was merely a rough frame devoid of any interior finishes, despite having 90% of the windows fully fitted. MacEachern noted that while the new owner initially tried to work with the existing layout, the scale of the required modifications ultimately necessitated a comprehensive structural redesign, rendering total demolition and rebuilding necessary for the desired property layout.The proposal was met with opposition from a neighbour The proposal has triggered formal pushback from a next door property owner who remain adamant in resisting the repeated cycle of construction and teardowns within the neighborhood. Architect Graham Goldsmith, owner of an adjacent property on Pocomo Road, made his qualms clear to the HDC during preliminary hearings. Goldsmith asked, "How many more buildings are we going to tear down in this neighborhood? It just goes on and on." Nantucket’s demolition-delay bylaw requires residential structures to be reviewed for reuse potential before a demolition permit can be issued.Goldsmith broached the demolition of a nearby 34-year-old mansion that belonged to Yankee Candle founder Michael J. Kittredge, questioning the sustainability of repeated neighborhood reconstructions. The regulatory power of the Historic District Commission remains strictly bound by municipal rules regardless of concerns about neighborhood consistency. HDC member Ray Pohl answered the neighborhood grievances by pointing out that the commission’s legal purview remains confined exclusively to reviewing external architecture and historical compatibility. Pohl maintained that any broader logistics, timelines, resource waste and teardown procedures remain outside the bounds of the HDC’s evaluation. As of October 8, 2024, neither Cohen nor representatives from the commission had issued any comments relevant to the upcoming scheduling or final decision on the pending demolition permit.You use AI every day. articles.body: A sprawling lakefront estate in Bellevue, Washington, that belongs to former NFL quarterback Russell Wilson and Grammy-winning singer Ciara, is officially in contract to change hands for $21.25 million, according to The Wall Street Journal, which cited a person familiar with the deal. When taken together with the separate sale of an adjacent parcel that held the couple's sports court, completed in 2022 for $9.75 million. The combined real estate transaction for the entire contiguous compound was set to reach $31 million.The transaction follows a two-year marketing effort done for the luxury compound. In April 2022, the 11,100-square-foot Mediterranean-style primary residence announced its arrival in the open real estate market for a premium asking price of $36 million which included the adjacent lot. This closely coincided with the high-profile offseason trade which saw the transfer of Wilson from the Seattle Seahawks to the Denver Broncos.After two separate market price adjustments, the initial asking price of the house, which stood at $28 million on its own, was brought down to $24.9 million, until it was secured by a buyer at a $21.25 million contract. Public property records suggest that Wilson, who married Ciara in July 2016 and shares three children with her, bought the main estate parcel for $6.7 million in 2015 and made a $14.6 million gain on the primary structure alone.What the mansion offers across three floors Overlooking Lake Washington and the Seattle skyline, the three-story residential estate sits on 1.06 acres of land. Inside, the floor plan accommodates six bedrooms and five full en-suite bathrooms. While the primary gourmet kitchen includes two Sub-Zero refrigerators and a gas range, all centred around a 14-foot prep island.A primary bedroom suite offers a private terrace access with a wood-burning fireplace and a dedicated alcove seating area. Its attached master bathroom suite boasts dual vanities alongside a soaking tub, a walk-in closet, and an adjoined vanity glamour room with its own fireplace. Elsewhere the home serves as a recreational haven fully equipped with a home theater, an au pair suite, a recording studio, two home offices, a sunroom, two separate fitness studios, and three specialized children’s playrooms.Luxury on the lakeside According to Carmen Gayton of Windermere Real Estate Co., who held the listing, the property has 164 feet of prime waterfront along Lake Washington with a boat dock, plus a tram down to the water or 77 steps for anyone who wants the exercise. While on the outside, the manicured grounds are replete with premier outdoor living, fire pits and an integrated hot tub. What stands out is a two-story treehouse which serves as a whimsical centerpiece with a spiral staircase and storybook-inspired green cladding. The couple added both the treehouse and the tram. Since, the estate sits along Lake Washington, shoreline improvements can also be subject to local permitting requirements. articles.title: In 2019, a Florida activist grew or foraged his food to test whether he could live without grocery stores; he completed one year without a grocery store
articles.summary: In an inspiring one-year project, activist Rob Greenfield foraged and grew all of his meals in Florida, avoiding grocery stores and showcasing the potential for urban foraging and food independence. Discover insights from his journey and the challenges he faced along the way.
articles.body: From November 11, 2018 to November 11, 2019, activist Rob Greenfield set out to see whether he could meet all of his food needs by growing or foraging for everything he ate. WUSF described how, for 365 days in Orlando, Florida, he avoided grocery stores, restaurants, takeout and food prepared by friends. He completed the project in November 2019 and later documented it in the book Food Freedom: A Year of Growing and Foraging 100 Percent of My Food, as noted in National Geographic’s profile of Rob Greenfield.Food Freedom project, November 11, 2018 to November 11, 2019National Geographic reported that Greenfield learned which plants worked well in Florida by talking with local growers, visiting community gardens, attending classes, watching YouTubers and reading books about local and native flora. He explained that this preparation, done before the project began, took him from knowing little about growing food in the region to being able to grow and forage all of his food. Greenfield relocated from San Diego to Orlando for the project, where the nonprofit Orlando Permaculture provided support, according to a January 2022 WUSF profile. With no land of his own in Florida, Greenfield built a 100-square-foot tiny house from repurposed materials in the backyard of Orlando herbalist Lisa Ray, who offered him the space.Project rules: no packaged, processed or shipped foodNothing packaged, processed or shipped became part of his food intake, according to the book's summary. Even vitamins and supplements were excluded. According to Greenfield's page on the project, he grew over 100 foods in his garden and over 200 foods in nature, including medicinal herbs and vitamins. The only thing he consumed but did not swallow was toothpaste, as he explained in an interview with WUSF.Protein and starch challenges, according to forager Hank Shaw, 2019This has been termed the “forager’s dilemma” by Shaw, who is a forager and author of cookbooks in California. Protein had to be obtained from legumes in the absence of hunting and fishing, but the state of Florida has very few wild legumes. Greenfield fished a few times per month, kept his catch frozen, and included pigeon peas and southern peas. Yucca, yams, and sweet potatoes were his sources of starch.Honey harvest: 75 pounds from three colonies after 100 daysBy the time of National Geographic's visit, more than 100 days into the project, Greenfield kept three honey bee colonies and had harvested 75 pounds of honey. He would also boil the salt from seawater. WUSF listed papaya, beets, spinach, sweet potatoes and moringa among the crops he raised. The rules governed the food he ate, and he also got an Instant Pot and containers to preserve the produce. The project page of Greenfield states that there were 15 gardens created for others, more than 200 fruit trees planted for the community, and more than 5,000 seed packs distributed free of cost. Some of this work began before the year started, so the figures cannot be taken as results of the 365 days alone.Vienna foraging survey: 458 residents, 64 percent of green space visitorsThe study Urban nature at the fingertips: Investigating wild food foraging to enable nature interactions of urban dwellers, by Christoph Schunko and Anjoulie Brandner in the journal Ambio, surveyed 458 residents of Vienna, Austria. Among the surveyed residents who visit public urban green spaces, 64 percent had previously foraged for wild food. Foraging frequency was related to the targeted plant species and their life forms. People who foraged more often reported a stronger connection to nature, had more childhood foraging experience and lived on the outskirts of the city. Social acceptance and lack of access to wild foods were perceived as barriers. That figure covers green space visitors in one city, not all urban residents or all cities. The scale differs sharply from Greenfield's project, in which he foraged more than 200 foods over a year.Ocean View Growing Grounds study, 2020: arsenic in chard, lead in strawberriesThe study Monitoring and mitigation of toxic heavy metals and arsenic accumulation in food crops: A case study of an urban community garden, published in Plant Direct in January 2020, repeatedly tested fruits and vegetables over four years at the Ocean View Growing Grounds community garden, on a formerly contaminated brownfield site in southeastern San Diego. Swiss chard grown directly in the ground contained arsenic at 0.80 mg/kg dry weight, while lettuce contained 0.42 mg/kg. Strawberries contained lead at 0.84 mg/kg dry weight. Tomatoes and Brussels sprouts showed no detectable levels of heavy metals or metalloids. Over the four-year sampling period, lead in the leaves of Black Mission fig trees measured 0.843 to 1.531 mg/kg dry weight, and in Mexican lime leaves 1.103 to 1.522 mg/kg dry weight, the study authors reported. When the raised beds made of uncontaminated soil were introduced, there were no detectable levels of heavy metals and metalloids in the crops.A Plantae summary of the same study, written by Mary Williams, noted that contaminants were found in the tree leaves but not in the fruits. The San Diego results do not describe the yards Greenfield used. Naturalist Steve Brill said in his interview with National Geographic that the lead settles in places where it is released, so he is careful about picking anything within 50 feet of heavy traffic. Greenfield told National Geographic that he never picks anything sprayed or contaminated. Phil Ackerman-Leist, an expert on pesticides, suggested that foragers in the city should use the same caution when gathering produce as they do while shopping at the produce aisle of a supermarket.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'He will never walk free’: Indian judge's letter promises child sex abuse survivor
articles.summary: In the emotional letter, the judge describes the survivor as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".
articles.body:
An Indian judge's moving letter praising a child rape survivor for her "courage" and assuring her that her abuser "will live in a cage for the rest of his life" is winning hearts in India.

Trial court Judge Rajani Ranga's letter addresses the 10-year-old, who was sexually abused on 23rd July 2023 when she was seven, as "Dear child" and describes her as "the bravest little girl this court has ever seen".

The trial court gave the convict a life sentence, emphasising that he would remain in prison for "the remainder of his natural life" and also awarded the survivor a compensation of 1.05m rupees ($10,941; £8,274).

At the end of her order, Judge Ranga said she "must address the child victim - not in the formal language of a judgment but as a judge who has heard her voice, who has read her words, and who has been moved by her courage".

"When you said 'Jab tak uncle buddhe na ho jaaye, tab tak unhe jail mein hi rakha jaaye [Keep the 'uncle' in jail until he grows old], this court listened. And this court has answered your plea," she wrote to the child survivor.

"Today, this court has ordered that the man you called 'uncle' will never walk free again. He will live in a cage for the rest of his life. He will grow old in that cage. He will die in that cage. He will never be able to hurt you, or your little sister, or any other child, ever again," she added.

Calling her "the bravest little girl", the judge praised her "for coming to court, pointing out the man who hurt her and telling the truth".

"The man you called 'uncle' did a very bad thing to you. But you did not stay quiet. You told your mother. And because you had the courage to speak, he will never be able to hurt another child again.

"The court can promise you that he will never see the sun as a free man again."

Concluding her letter, the judge said the "court cannot give you back your childhood", but advised her to "now live your life. Go to school. Make friends. Laugh. Play. Dream. This court will always remember your courage".

Judge Ranga's letter is part of the order that was announced on 11 July, but as cases of child sexual assault are tried in special Pocso (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) courts, their judgments are never made public to protect the identities of the victims.

It came to light after it was reproduced recently in a Delhi high court order which rejected the convict's appeal for bail and suspension of sentence. The high court order named the convict, who is an adult, but gave no other details about him.

Describing Judge Ranga's letter as "a message of encouragement" to the child, the high court judges ordered the Delhi State Legal Authority to print out a copy and give it to the child along with the compensation money.

The emotional letter has moved many Indians who have shared it on social media, describing it as "a rarity" and "a ray of hope" and praising the judge.

Many have also expressed sorrow at the horrific nature of the crime where a child was sexually abused when she was just seven.

The judge's letter may be rare, but campaigners say the seven-year-old child's case is not a rarity - more than 69,000 Pocso cases were recorded in India in 2024 alone, according to government crime data .

And studies reveal that as in a majority of cases, abusers are known to the victims and are often trusted persons and care-givers, many cases are not even reported to the authorities.

Survivors say such abuse can scar them forever and affect their entire life.

In her order, Judge Ranga also addressed the issue of how such an assault can have a permanent impact on a child.

After "evaluating the nature of the crime, the depth of suffering, and the lifelong impact on the victim child", she said her order was "an attempt to heal and restore" the child.

articles.title: In 2022, Schiphol put 2,571 kilos of recycled plastic beneath an airport road, creating room for 43,200 litres of rainwater and an expected 30-year life
articles.summary: In 2022, Amsterdam Airport Schiphol constructed a groundbreaking road made from 2,571 kilos of recycled plastic, designed to hold rainwater and expected to last for 30 years. This innovative project aims to address plastic waste and flooding issues simultaneously.
articles.body: Roads have a silent tendency to exacerbate floods. When rain strikes a sealed surface, it cannot be absorbed and rushes towards drains that were not designed to handle heavy precipitation. In the meantime, plastic trash continues to accumulate in the majority of nations, with far too little of it recycled. In the Netherlands, where water issues are a daily concern, engineers have been trying to address both problems with a single piece of infrastructure.In 2022, Amsterdam Airport Schiphol constructed a section of road and several parking bays from recycled plastic collected at the airport. The first stretch contained 2,571 kilos of recycled plastic and was designed to store 43,200 litres of water. The plastic elements were anticipated to endure roughly 30 years, according to Schiphol. In effect, Schiphol built a road that doubles as a hidden water-storage system, using recycled plastic from the airport. This is a pilot project, not a typical construction method, and the figures explain why road experts are taking notice.What Schiphol builtNear the Kaagbaan Tunnel, Schiphol, in collaboration with PlasticRoad, PreZero and VolkerWessels Infra Schiphol, constructed the road. Prefabricated plastic parts with empty gaps inside replace poured asphalt. On top of this is a thin coating of crushed stone which protects the plastic from wear and prevents the surface becoming slippery when it rains. “The surface drives like asphalt,” Schiphol explains.The water-storage system begins with the hollow structure. Rain that falls on the road is collected, filtered and allowed to slowly soak into the earth. The area inside acts as a buffer in heavy weather, and Schiphol says the technique also increases groundwater levels and prevents pollution from vehicles seeping into the land beside the road.These numbers are simple enough to visualise. Storing 43,200 litres in a road made from 2,571 kilos of plastic means holding about 16.8 litres of water for every kilo of material. That is equivalent to 216 standard 200-litre drums. All of this is hidden away behind a surface that vehicles normally travel over.Why plastic is importantPlastic waste is a global challenge, and much of it is not recycled. According to the OECD’s Global Plastics Outlook, plastic waste surged from 156 million tonnes in 2000 to 353 million tonnes in 2019. In 2019, the OECD estimated that 9% of global plastic waste was ultimately recycled, 19% was incinerated, almost 50% went to sanitary landfills and the remaining 22% was disposed of in uncontrolled dumpsites, burnt in open pits or leaked into the environment.A road that eats plastic looks promising in that context. Schiphol took garbage from its activities, which keeps transport short and gives the material a local use. Schiphol says the elements are expected to last around 30 years and can then be processed for reuse or, if that is not possible, used as raw material for new elements. Plastic that is sealed into a durable structure and then recycled again is a vastly different conclusion than plastic that winds up in a landfill or a river. The road is also a bigger promise. Schiphol has declared that it aspires to be a waste-free and emission-free airport by 2030, and it reuses almost 70 per cent of its demolition materials. The plastic road is one example of the airport's broader effort to reduce waste and emissions.What remains uncertainSchiphol designed the project as a one-year pilot to measure wear, maintenance needs and the general quality of the road surface, just as it does with its standard roads. The pilot was intended to help assess how the system performs under intensive airport use, while the 30-year figure remains an expected design life rather than a demonstrated service life. If the pilot is successful, the airport said it plans to develop more roadways with this type of surface.The other issue is wear. Any road that contains plastic raises fears that microscopic particles of plastic will be shed as the wheels grind over it. That is one reason for the stone layer on top of the Schiphol design. The Virginia Transportation Research Council found that field trials mixing modified asphalt with recycled plastic could match a standard mix in durability and outperform it in resistance to rutting and cracking. Researchers also developed lab methods to look for microplastics in pavement wear that could be washed away by stormwater.The work focuses on using plastic in asphalt, not on modular elements such as those used at Schiphol. But it does suggest that engineers increasingly treat wear particles as something to measure rather than ignore. The pilot shows how recycled plastic can be incorporated into airport road infrastructure while creating space for temporary rainwater storage. We will have to see how the road holds up after years of intensive use. If the pilot passes that test, plastic roads might be a valuable weapon in the fight against both flooding and waste, and until then they remain a promising experiment worth watching.You use AI every day. articles.title: Overdue fines to be scrapped at libraries in Devon
articles.summary: Devon County Council hopes the change will encourage more people to borrow books.
articles.body:
Library users across Devon will no longer face fines for overdue books from Thursday.

Devon County Council said this comes after more than 25,000 people responded to a consultation on the future of Devon's libraries.

It added all existing overdue charges would also be removed, giving library users a clean slate.

Councillor Cheryl Cottle-Hunkin, Devon County Council cabinet member responsible for libraries, said: "Libraries are at the heart of our communities, and removing overdue fines makes it easier and encourages more people to borrow books, discover a love of reading, and enjoy everything else our libraries have to offer."

Libraries Unlimited, the charity commissioned to run Devon's libraries, removed late fees for children and young people in 2022 to help remove barriers to reading.

Cottle-Hunkin added: "Where fines have been scrapped elsewhere, the results have been overwhelmingly positive, helping to remove barriers not just financially, but psychologically too.

"Libraries change lives, and we want as many people as possible to benefit from them."

Alex Kittow, chief executive officer at Libraries Unlimited, said: "Our hope is that this brings people back into libraries who haven't been borrowing books because of overdue fines on their account.

"We also want to remind people that books are expensive, and we do need them back so that hundreds of thousands of people across Devon can benefit from the joy of reading for free."

Libraries Unlimited said loan periods would remain in place, and people would still be asked to return or renew items when they are due.

It said reservation fees and charges for lost books would also remain.

articles.title: Met Police submits Grenfell Tower fire investigation files to CPS
articles.summary: The force is seeking charges against 54 individuals and 20 companies over the 2017 tower block fire that killed 72 people.
articles.body:
The Metropolitan Police has submitted its final investigation file into the Grenfell Tower fire to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), seeking charges against 54 individuals and 20 companies.

These include corporate manslaughter, gross negligence manslaughter, health and safety offences, fraud and fraud-related offences and misconduct in public office.

The Met described the case into the fire which killed 72 people at the tower block in North Kensington, west London, as one of the "most complex investigations ever undertaken by any UK law enforcement agency".

The CPS said charging decisions would be made before the 10th anniversary of the disaster, which is on 14 June 2027.

A public inquiry report released in 2024 found the fire was avoidable and set out how a chain of failures across government and the private sector led to the disaster.

The Met's investigation, Operation Northleigh, has run in parallel with the public inquiry into the disaster, but detectives waited for the inquiry to publish its findings before completing their work.

Some bereaved families and survivors have said this delayed justice, but it allowed police to consider the inquiry's often highly technical conclusions.

Grenfell United, a bereaved families and survivors group, said "no family should have to fight this hard, for this long, for justice".

"It has taken more than nine years to get here. Nine years, and no one has been held criminally accountable for the deaths of our 72 loved ones.

"We want those responsible to face justice. If people are found guilty of crimes that cost our loved ones their lives, we want to see them behind bars.

"Only then will people see that there are real consequences for what happened at Grenfell."

Joe Powell, MP for Kensington and Bayswater, welcomed the news but said bereaved families and survivors "have already waited an agonising nine years for justice".

"My position remains clear that we must do everything in our power to ensure that justice is delivered as swiftly as possible.

"I will continue working with government ministers to ensure everything is done to avoid any further delays," he added.

The charred remains of Grenfell Tower were a crime scene for 14 months, during which forensic teams scoured the building for evidence of why the fire spread so quickly.

Detectives commissioned their own laboratory tests and examined thousands of pieces of debris from the fire, including the fridge which malfunctioned in a fourth-floor flat, from where the flames spread rapidly to the rest of the building.

The evidence has been kept in a warehouse at a secret location, which the BBC visited last year.

Police have investigated the actions of 15,000 people across 700 organisations or companies and taken 14,700 statements.

The investigation has also examined 45,000 documents, images and exhibits.

The files sent to the CPS include examples of this evidence, as well as reports containing more than two million words.

Deputy assistant commissioner Kevin Southworth said a team of 220 investigators had worked hard on the case but he appreciates "it has taken nine years to get to this point".

"As we have said before, this is one of the most complex investigations ever undertaken by any UK law enforcement agency – the scale is truly enormous.

"While we know this has had a significant impact on those waiting for answers, it has necessarily taken this long to ensure our investigation is meticulous and presents the very best possible evidence to the CPS for charging decisions," he added.

The CPS will decide whether there is a realistic prospect of conviction, as well as considering whether bringing charges is in the public interest.

In anticipation of possible criminal proceedings, the Met has said it is building a £2m replica of a section of the tower, which is being dismantled, to help future jurors understand its layout.

Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS special crime and counter terrorism division, said it marked "an important step".

"We recognise that the journey to this point has been long and difficult.

"Charging decisions will be made independently by CPS prosecutors following a thorough and careful review of all the evidence gathered by the Metropolitan Police Service," he added.

articles.title: Ex-Pakistan SSG commando, highly trained LeT terrorist, Pahalgam mastermind: Who was Hashim Moosa; killed in J&K encounter
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorist Mohammad Asif alias Hashim Moosa, wanted for his alleged role in the 2025 Pahalgam terror
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) terrorist Mohammad Asif alias Hashim Moosa, wanted for his alleged role in the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, was killed in an encounter with security forces in Jammu and Kashmir's Budgam district on Wednesday.Moosa was killed during a joint operation by the Indian Army, Jammu and Kashmir Police and the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) in the Korag area of Yousmarg. His body was later recovered from the general area of Palmaidan along with war-like stores, according to the Army's Chinar Corps.Moosa's killing has brought renewed focus on the background of the LeT terrorist, who security agencies had identified as one of the key suspects in the Pahalgam attack and linked to other terror attacks in Jammu and Kashmir.Who was Hashim Moosa?Moosa was a Pakistani LeT terrorist wanted in connection with the April 22, 2025 Pahalgam terror attack, in which 26 people were killed.Former Jammu and Kashmir DGP S.P. Vaid on Wednesday described Moosa as a highly trained terrorist and alleged that his footprints had surfaced in several attacks in Jammu and Kashmir, including attacks in the Poonch region and the Pahalgam attack.Vaid said Moosa was considered the mastermind of the Pahalgam attack and described him as a Pakistani national and a commando-trained terrorist specialising in jungle warfare and guerrilla operations.Is Hashim Moosa an ex-SSG commando?One of the key aspects of Moosa's background now being examined is his alleged connection with Pakistan's military.News agency ANI also quotes security agency sources stating that Moosa had served as a para-commando in Pakistan's Special Service Group (SSG) where he held the rank of Havildar. Following his retirement from the SSG in 2023, he joined the terrorist outfit Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) and infiltrated into India.Vaid described Moosa as a highly trained commando specialising in ambushes and guerrilla-style attacks. He alleged that Moosa's footprints had been seen in attacks in Poonch, DKG, Bhimber Gali, the Gulmarg attack and the Reasi attack on pilgrims.The alleged SSG connection could shed further light on Moosa's training and his role within the LeT network, but the military background remains a matter of investigation.ALSO READ: 'Save Democracy March' announced: INDIA bloc projects unity amid SIR row, targets PM Modi, Amit ShahWhat attacks is Moosa linked to?The Pahalgam attack took place on April 22, 2025, when terrorists targeted tourists at Baisaran Valley. Twenty-six people were killed in the attack.According to the ANI report, Moosa was named as one of the key suspects in the attack and had been wanted by Jammu and Kashmir Police.The National Investigation Agency later chargesheeted seven accused in the case, including Pakistan-based LeT and The Resistance Front (TRF), which it charged as a legal entity for allegedly planning, facilitating and executing the attack.The NIA's 1,597-page chargesheet also named Pakistani handler Sajid Jatt as an accused.The agency had said its investigation detailed the Pakistan-based conspiracy and the roles of those accused in the attack.How was Moosa killed?Security forces launched Operation Korag in the Yousmarg area of Budgam following specific intelligence inputs about terrorist movement.During the joint search operation, troops observed suspicious activity and challenged the terrorists. The terrorists opened fire, triggering an encounter in which Moosa was killed.The operation involved the Indian Army, Jammu and Kashmir Police and the CRPF.The search operation continued after the encounter, with security personnel checking the surrounding area for any additional terrorist presence. During the search, Moosa's body was recovered from Palmaidan along with war-like stores, according to the Chinar Corps.Pahalgam victim's daughter calls it ‘one chapter’ closedThe killing also drew a reaction from Asavari Jagdale, daughter of Pahalgam attack victim Santosh Jagdale.Speaking to ANI, Jagdale thanked the Army and intelligence agencies for the operation and recalled the April 22 attack in which 26 people were killed.She described the killing as a step towards justice but said the legal process must continue until the case reaches its final verdict.“I would say that one chapter of the case has ended,” she said.Jagdale also urged security agencies to continue operations against terrorists and said the 26 families would consider the case fully closed only after completion of the legal proceedings.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Exercise Jai se Vijay’: Army Helicopters Turn NH-911 into Military Runway Near Pak Border Mission Ready
articles.summary: A strategically important stretch of National Highway-911 near Dantour in Rajasthan, close to the India-Pakistan International Border, was transformed
articles.body: A strategically important stretch of National Highway-911 near Dantour in Rajasthan, close to the India-Pakistan International Border, was transformed into a temporary military runway on Tuesday as the Indian Army conducted ‘Exercise Jai se Vijay’, demonstrating its operational preparedness, mobility and ability to rapidly adapt to changing battlefield requirements.The exercise was conducted by the Sapta Shakti Command, with Rudra, Dhruv and Chetak helicopters demonstrating exceptional operational agility during a series of highway landing and take-off drills. The military aviation activity turned a normally busy stretch of the national highway into a temporary operating surface for Army helicopters.The exercise was conducted under the theme “Mission Ready, Future Ready”, highlighting the Army’s focus on maintaining a high level of operational readiness while developing the flexibility required for future battlefield scenarios.During the exercise, the helicopters executed precision landings and take-offs from the designated highway stretch. The activity demonstrated the capability of Army Aviation assets to operate from locations other than conventional military airbases and established helipads.The use of a national highway as an alternative operating surface is particularly significant in strategically sensitive border areas. In a contingency, conventional airfields or helipads could be unavailable, damaged or unsuitable for immediate operations. In such circumstances, suitably prepared stretches of highways and other dual-use infrastructure can provide additional options for military mobility and aviation operations.The exercise also demonstrated the importance of rapid response and situational awareness. The ability to quickly relocate aviation assets and operate from dispersed locations can support the movement of troops, equipment and essential supplies, besides providing greater flexibility during military contingencies.Operating helicopters in the desert environment of western Rajasthan presents its own set of challenges. Strong winds, blowing sand, high temperatures, dust and changing visibility can make aviation operations demanding. Conducting landing and take-off drills on a relatively narrow highway surface therefore requires precision from pilots and close coordination between the aircrew, ground crew and other elements involved in the exercise.The highway was prepared and regulated for the military activity while prescribed safety procedures were followed. The controlled exercise provided an opportunity to validate procedures for operating helicopters from alternative locations and to assess the coordination required between aviation and ground elements.The Rudra armed helicopter, Dhruv Advanced Light Helicopter and Chetak helicopter brought together different aviation capabilities during the exercise. Their operations on the highway demonstrated the versatility of Army Aviation assets and their ability to support ground forces in challenging terrain.The exercise further highlighted the growing importance of dual-use infrastructure in modern military planning. Strategically located highways can potentially serve both civilian and military purposes, providing additional operational flexibility without depending exclusively on permanent military infrastructure.For forces deployed along the western border, mobility and the ability to rapidly disperse assets are important elements of operational preparedness. The exercise demonstrated how aviation platforms can be integrated with alternative infrastructure to maintain responsiveness during contingencies.The successful conduct of Exercise Jai se Vijay provided a practical demonstration of the Sapta Shakti Command’s rapid response capability, operational flexibility and mission readiness in the demanding desert environment.The highway landing exercise thus reinforced the message of “Mission Ready, Future Ready”, showcasing the Indian Army’s focus on agility, mobility, situational awareness and the effective utilisation of available infrastructure for enhanced operational preparedness along the western frontier.

articles.title: Jay Slater's mum says retracing his steps has given her 'more closure'
articles.summary: Debbie Duncan went to Tenerife to trace her son Jay's final steps before his death in 2024.
articles.body:
The mother of Jay Slater, who died after he went missing in Tenerife, has said retracing his footsteps was "very tough and emotional" but had given her "more closure".

Jay, 19, and from Oswaldtwistle in Lancashire, went missing on 17 June 2024 after attending a music festival in Playa de las Americas on the Spanish island, and was found dead after a 29-day search.

His mother, Debbie Duncan, told BBC Radio Lancashire she hoped after watching a forthcoming documentary on the case, people "may well believe the facts".

The first episode of the Channel Five series "Cause of Death", which will explore the manhunt and huge social media interest around the case, will air at 21:00 BST on Wednesday.

An inquest into Jay's death ruled it was a "tragic accident," and entirely without third party influence.

He had fallen in a "particularly dangerous area", and suffered skull fractures and brain trauma that killed him instantly.

Debbie said retracing her son's steps helped her, because "we could look at the terrain in more detail".

"It was the timeline for me, from his location... to him saying 'I don't know where I am, I am lost'. So that was important to me, to time it."

The episode retraces his steps alongside forensic pathologist Richard Shepherd, who carried out Jay's postmortem when his body was returned to the UK.

"Having Dr Shepherd there to talk more about his injuries was just really good," Debbie said, adding he had been able "to explain it in more simple terms".

"It was very tough and emotional going back there, but we have got more closure. Obviously I didn't question for one minute it was an accident," she said.

She said the family were "all coping in different ways" since Jay's death.

"I'm trying to keep busy, and I am in contact with other bereaved families.

"I can't say it helps, but talking to other parents who have gone through losing their children, you know you are not on your own."

Last year, she called for Jay's Law to prevent the online trolling of grieving families.

Following his disappearance, a number of theories about what had happened to him began to circulate on social media.

She said the law would be "aimed at tech companies" and obligate them "to take down misinformation".

She added that "the conspiracies were wild".

"People have said you are taking away our freedom of speech.

"It's not about freedom of speech. It's downright bullying. They know the facts but they don't want to believe them, they just go along withe their own narrative."

She said "the right people were listening" to her campaign.

But she said it had not got easier to live without Jay, adding: "It seems to get harder to be honest."

articles.title: North Wales Police detective pleads guilty to 'upskirting'
articles.summary: He was a lead investigator in the case of two-year-old Ethan Ives-Griffiths who was murdered.
articles.body:
A former detective has admitted taking pictures beneath the clothing of a child without consent - also known as "upskirting".

Lee Harshey-Jones, 45, pleaded guilty to one charge of voyeurism and one of perverting the course of justice by applying a factory reset to his mobile phone to conceal evidence on 11 June 2026, in Colwyn Bay, Conwy county.

He was a detective constable and lead investigator in the case of two-year-old Ethan Ives-Griffiths , whose grandparents were jailed for murder last year, and has given evidence in other high-profile murder trials in north Wales.

Harshey-Jones was given conditional bail following a hearing at Chester Crown Court, and will be sentenced on 19 November.

He was suspended by North Wales Police after his arrest, and has since resigned from the force.

Harshey-Jones also pleaded guilty to a charge of corrupt or improper exercise of his police powers and privileges by looking up his own incident on the computer log.

Ryan Donoghue, defending, asked for a pre-sentence report for his client, who he said was of previous good character.

He was told by Recorder Mark Ford KC he must sign the sex offenders register.

The recorder added: "The fact that I have adjourned the case for a pre-sentence report should not be taken by you as any indication to you as to what sentence will be passed on these serious counts."

Operating equipment beneath clothing without consent is an offence under the Sexual Offences Act 2003.

North Wales Police said the former officer had resigned from the force.

The force added that as criminal proceedings and misconduct protocols remained active and it was unable to provide comment at this time.

articles.title: Flight to Israel diverts to Saudi Arabia after violent cockpit altercation
articles.summary: An apparent fight between pilots on a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel forced an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia amid concern of a possible hijacking a...
articles.body:
A FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Israel was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday after an apparent altercation in the cockpit, raising concerns about a possible hijacking and prompting Israel to scramble fighter jets.

Israeli media outlets, citing security officials, said the incident stemmed from a fight between the commercial plane's two pilots and that everyone on board was safe after it landed in Tabuk, where there is a civilian airport adjacent to a Saudi military base.

The Jerusalem Post reported that one pilot tried to hijack the plane but was subdued by other members of the flight crew and passengers, citing an unnamed Israeli official who told the newspaper that a "major disaster was narrowly avoided."

A female passenger told Israel Hayom that one pilot was stabbed during the brawl, and Israeli passengers intervened to stop the fighting.

"There are people here with shirts covered in blood," she said, describing the incident as "very stressful." Videos shared on social media corroborated her account, showing at two men on the floor with blood smeared on and around them.

A passenger speaking to the Jerusalem Post said one pilot stabbed the other and tried to force him out of the cockpit as the plane began to plummet. The passenger told the newspaper a group of Israeli passengers near the front of the aircraft rushed to fight the attacker as the plane lost altitude.

The witness said the intervening passengers shouted at two off-duty pilots at the back of the plane "to run and take control" of it, and one of them did so after the passengers managed to remove the attacker from the cockpit.

Israeli sources told the Post the would-be hijacker was an Omani national. There was no immediate confirmation of the details from Israeli or Saudi officials.

The crew of FlyDubai flight 1073, a Boeing 737 Max 8 aircraft, transmitted an emergency alert shortly after takeoff on Wednesday, according to publicly available flight tracking information.

CBS News' British partner network BBC News said flight tracking data showed the aircraft plummeted more than 17,000 feet in two minutes around 8:21 a.m. local time.

Yasmin Abukasis, whose daughter was on the flight, told journalists at Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion Airport, where the plane had been due to land, that her daughter heard screaming as a pilot called for help.

"The plane start to lose control. So all the people, they scream," she said.

A regional official briefed on the incident told the Associated Press a fight broke out in the cockpit apparently involving the pilots, but the official did not say what had caused the altercation. The AP cited a second official confirming that Israel had scrambled warplanes, fearing a possible hijacking of the plane carrying dozens of Israeli citizens.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon. Netanyahu's office later issued a statement saying the situation was under control and Israel was working to bring the passengers home.

The BBC reported that a recovery flight was on its way to Tabuk to pick up the passengers from the diverted plane.

Emergency landings for personnel reasons are rare but not unheard of. In 2022, two Air France pilots were suspended after fighting in the cockpit on a Geneva-to-Paris flight, though the plane landed as scheduled in the French capital.

FlyDubai is the lower-cost sister carrier of the United Arab Emirates state-owned flagship carrier Emirates airlines. The UAE has become a popular vacation destination for Israeli tourists since the two nations normalized ties in 2020.

Israel has not experienced a plane hijacking in decades, but it maintains some of the strictest airport security in the world.

Israel's far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, in a social media post on Wednesday, said "the naive notion that our enemies value life and that we should have mercy on them received another reminder this morning in the form of a terrorist who planned to crash a plane and murder the 180 Israelis on board."

Israeli politician Benny Gantz, who is running in upcoming Israeli elections but polling badly, wrote on X : "It's still too early to know what the sequence of events was in this morning's Flydubai flight to Israel, but it's already clear that Israelis are a rare breed."

"The resourcefulness and courage displayed by the passengers on this flight, in the face of clear mortal danger, are exactly the stuff our people are made of," he said.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also posted about the incident Wednesday , saying: "Well this had everyone in the Middle East (esp Israel) on FULL ALERT this morning."

"Glad it wasn't more serious," he added, "but having pilots inflight detouring to 'fist city' not your ordinary experience."

articles.title: Kurt Cobain’s Olympia apartment, where he lived from 1989 to 1991 and wrote some of Nirvana’s best-known music, is now an Airbnb; fans can stay inside a preserved piece of rock history for $250 to $300 a night
articles.summary: Nirvana frontman Kurt Cobain’s downtown Olympia apartment, where he lived while producing much of the iconic 1991 album Nevermind, is now listed as a
articles.body: Nirvana frontman Kurt Cobain’s downtown Olympia apartment, where he lived while producing much of the iconic 1991 album Nevermind, is now listed as a short-term rental on Airbnb, according to Fox13. The apartment, located near East Bay Waterfront Park, offers short-term stays with a two-night minimum, with more availability for summer bookings. The apartment retains some of its original fixtures and memorabilia, along with modern amenities. A night in the apartment now costs $250 to $300 on Airbnb, Realtor.com reports. Rock ‘n’ roll fanatics now have the rare opportunity to experience the space where Kurt Cobain produced chart-topping music and called home.A triplex downtown buildingLocated on Pear Street in Olympia, WA, about 60 miles south of Seattle, this apartment was built around 1914, according to the Olympia Historical Society. It has three apartments, two facing the street and one at the rear.Kurt Cobain lived in this triplex building between 1989 and 1991, and it is now filled with Nirvana photos and memorabilia.Cobain wrote ‘about 75% of his total lifetime output’ while living here, according to the historical society. That stretch runs from the period around Nirvana’s debut album Bleach into the months before Nevermind.The listing describes the stay as a quiet downtown studio with a ‘unique opportunity to experience a one-of-a-kind vibe for musicians, artists and writers’. It is ‘an eclectic space with musical history’. The Olympia studio comes fully furnished with a queen bed and a serene backyard with a cherry tree. Wi-Fi and cable are also provided. The property is a short walk from East Bay Waterfront Park.The wall that named a songThe apartment’s best-known story involves Kathleen Hanna, singer of Bikini Kill. In August 1990, after a night out with Cobain, she wrote ‘Kurt smells like Teen Spirit’ on his bedroom wall.Teen Spirit was a deodorant. Cobain did not know that, so he read the line as something closer to a slogan, and later borrowed it as a title. The song itself came later. Cobain began writing ‘Smells Like Teen Spirit’ a few weeks before Nirvana recorded Nevermind in 1991. So the Pear Street wall also made its own contribution to Cobain’s musical career.Nirvana released three studio albums and disbanded in April 1994 after Cobain’s death. The band has reportedly sold more than 75 million records worldwide. Nevermind alone has passed 30 million copies.Cobain moved out of Pear Street 35 years ago, before that album made him famous. The apartment sits in a residential stretch of downtown Olympia, and the listing puts guests in the same rooms where the band’s early material took shape.The best part is that Cobain and his then-girlfriend, Tracy Marander, only paid about $137 for both rent and utilities for this triplex, according to YouTube travel creator Dave Seminara. Now, three and a half decades later, the place itself fetches around $300 for a night.A cosy stayThe quiet Olympia getaway has attracted hundreds of visitors. The listing has a 4.8-star rating. The bathroom comes with hot water, bath essentials and cleaning products. The bedroom has bed linen, an iron, hangers and a wardrobe. There is also an entertainment unit with a TV, as well as books and other reading materials. There is a smoke alarm, carbon monoxide alarm, fire extinguisher and first aid kit for safety. The kitchen comes with a fridge, freezer, coffee maker, toaster, microwave and cooking basics such as pots and pans, oil, salt and pepper. There is also adequate crockery and cutlery.Visitors also mention the proximity to places to eat and explore in downtown Olympia.‘A very special place, still can’t quite believe we stayed here. Many of the fixtures and fittings that Kurt would have used are intact (the shower, sink, taps, some door handles, the kitchen cabinets etc.) and probably much more. Many notable photos are also taken in the Garden...’ one visitor wrote.Another said, ‘For any fan of the grunge legend Kurt Cobain this is a must stay! The history of this apartment is legendary it was during the time of Bleach and beginning of Nevermind (aka this time period as Kurt’s happiest). They kept the unit as it would have been back in his day. It makes it an experience to live in this relic. To see how a ‘rockstar’ would live.’You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Russia launches largest attack on Ukraine energy infrastructure since spring
articles.summary: In total 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings and railways also targeted, the Ukrainian PM says.
articles.body:
Russia has launched the largest attack on Ukraine's energy infrastructure since the spring, primarily targeting Kyiv and the surrounding region, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi has said.

At least five people were killed in overnight attacks across the country, including a child in the Kyiv region, Koretskyi said.

The strikes also impacted people's power supplies, with Ukraine's biggest private energy firm, DTEK, saying power to 8,000 homes had been restored following "a difficult night" for the capital.

The Russian defence ministry said one of its targets was the Trypilska power station, the largest supplier of electricity to Kyiv.

In a statement on Telegram, Koretskyi said: "Since the summer, there has effectively not been a single day without enemy attacks on our energy infrastructure.

"However, a mass and combined attack of this scale has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season."

Ukraine has been expecting another protracted Russian assault on the country's energy grid. It has happened every winter so far since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

In total 11 regions of the country were attacked overnight, with residential buildings, social infrastructure, civilian enterprises and railways also targeted, Koretskyi said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said there were strikes on critical infrastructure in the Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, Kirovohrad and Rivne regions.

On Wednesday, some households in the Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Sumy, Kyiv and Kharkiv regions remained without power, Ukraine's energy ministry said.

State-owned grid operator Ukrenegro advised residents not to use powerful electrical appliances between the hours of 10:00 and 16:00 local time as electricity supplies were lower than usual.

Russia's defence ministry said it had launched massive overnight strikes on Ukrainian facilities.

It said its targets included the Trypilska thermal power plant, located some 40km from Kyiv, and claimed the plant supplied electricity to Ukrainian defence facilities.

The operator of the plant, Centrenergo, confirmed that the plant had been damaged in a Russian attack and that it was assessing the scale of the damage.

In Kyiv, people woke to find the city blanketed by thick, acrid smoke after a night punctuated by the sound of explosions. An air raid alert was still on and the distant sound of air defence gunfire echoed through the murky atmosphere.

Residents in several districts were advised to close their windows until the smoke cleared.

Among those killed in the overnight strikes was a child whose body was found under the rubble of a house, Kyiv regional governor Timur Tkachenko said.

Kyiv Mayor Vitaly Klischko said three people were killed in total in the capital, including a Ukrainian utility company worker who was killed at a warehouse building.

Another person was killed in the Mykolaiv region, acting regional governor Heorhiy Reshetilov said.

Two more people were also killed in the north-eastern Sumy region on Tuesday, governor Oleh Hryhorov said. A school was also hit there in a separate strike, he added.

Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.

articles.title: Botswana condemned for slaughtering elephants for independence celebrations
articles.summary: The government authorises the hunting of 23 elephants and dozens of other wild animals for independence day feasts.
articles.body:
Animal rights activists have criticised Botswana's decision to authorise the killing of 23 elephants to provide meat for independence celebrations.

The southern African country, home to the world's largest elephant population, is holding nationwide festivities on Wednesday to mark the 60th anniversary of independence from Britain.

A licence issued by the Ministry of Environment and Tourism, seen by local media, authorises the hunting of 23celephants and other wild animals for "complimentary purposes".

The Botswana-based Elephant Protection Society warns the decision could undermine conservation, with its chairman Oaitse Nawa telling the BBC elephants needed greater protection.

He warned that slaughtering elephants for celebratory feasting could encourage poaching by creating the impression that killing elephants is acceptable when sanctioned by government.

"Elephants have lost their social structures because they are always being pushed from one place to another by gunshots," Nawa said.

Several social media users in the country have also expressed concerns about eating the game meat amid an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, which has prompted authorities to impose measures to contain its spread.

Tshenatshe Monwela, an elder in Maun, a tourism town in north-western Botswana told local media that his community should have received buffalo instead.

He argued that elephants had particular cultural and ecological significance and that Botswana's historic role in protecting the country's wildlife and livestock should have been recognised in the government's allocation of meat for the anniversary celebrations.

Elephants use medicinal plants to treat themselves, researchers find

Botswana's government has organised a series of events to mark the country's diamond jubilee, including a carnival in the capital, Gaborone, as well as cultural performances, concerts and sporting events.

The game meat is expected to be served as part of the traditional feasting associated with the Independence Day celebrations.

The 23 elephants were allocated in eight districts across the country.

It was not immediately clear how many of the animals had been killed by Wednesday morning. The BBC has asked the government for comment.

But local media published images from different parts of Botswana showing residents gathering around elephant carcasses, some with knives in hand and sharing the meat.

In Chobe, a wildlife-rich district in northern Botswana near the borders with Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe, a local MP raised concerns after residents reportedly collected portions directly from a carcass at a school.

He said the system risked creating congestion and disadvantaging elderly people, pregnant women and people with disabilities, and suggested the meat should instead be processed into 5kg or 10kg packages to improve hygiene and ensure fairer distribution.

"For the sake of dignity, fairness and public hygiene, we respectfully call on the hunter and the relevant leadership to ensure that future distributions are properly organised," MP Simasiku Mapulanga posted on Facebook, attaching photos of people scrambling for meat around an elephant carcass.

Elephant meat is common in some wildlife-rich communities, particularly when meat from legal hunts is distributed locally, but it is not an everyday staple.

Botswana also tightly regulates game meat, and its legal possession generally depends on proving it came from a lawful hunt.

The decision has reignited a long-running and often heated debate in Botswana over how the country manages its huge elephant population.

Botswana has more than 130,000 elephants and communities living alongside them have long complained about animals destroying crops, damaging property and sometimes killing people.

The government has defended regulated hunting as one way of managing the elephant population and human-wildlife conflict while generating income for communities.

The country banned trophy hunting in 2014 under former President Ian Khama but lifted the restrictions five years later under his successor, Mokgweetsi Masisi.

Hunting has continued under President Duma Boko, who defeated Masisi in elections in 2024.

The government says proceeds from hunting supports conservation and local development.

Minister of Environment and Tourism Wynter Mmolotsi told parliament last year that special elephant quotas raised 15.6m pula ($1.1m; £820,000) in 2025 for projects in areas where elephants are found.

But conservation organisations have questioned whether the level of hunting is sustainable.

Supporters of Botswana's hunting policy, however, argue that international criticism often overlooks the costs borne by rural communities living alongside one of the world's biggest concentrations of elephants.

They say elephants destroy crops and infrastructure and pose a danger to people, particularly as their range increasingly overlaps with farms and settlements.

articles.title: Residents fear new rules could mean dangerous cladding is left on flats
articles.summary: The government says it hopes the changes will speed up the process of removing cladding.
articles.body:
When Natasha Parcell first got her foot on the property ladder little did she expect to be one of the latest victims of the cladding crisis.

"I was really excited to have something of my own," she says, "[but] very quickly in the first year I was told it was actually no longer safe or mortgageable."

The 33-year-old is currently living in a hotel after being evacuated from her flat, in east London, following a fatal fire in her tower block earlier this month .

All she was able to take with her were some plastic bags filled with clothes.

The blaze came just a day after residents got approval to have all the flammable cladding on the building removed.

However, she is worried new rules - which come into force on Wednesday - may allow the developer Barratt to backtrack on that decision. The rules state cladding can remain in place on blocks if the risk is deemed to be "tolerable".

"To find out that they're [the government] trying to change the standards in which they might remediate our buildings is quite terrifying," says Parcell.

"Literally two weeks ago, we had a fatal fire in our building and we're still being told that they might change the rules and it might be a tolerable risk. I just don't understand when human life, or my life, became a tolerable risk to anybody."

The developer of Parcell's flat, Barratt Redrow, says despite the new rules it still intends to remove all the flammable cladding on her tower block as soon as possible.

It is nearly ten years since the Grenfell Tower fire, but almost 3,000 tower blocks in the UK with dangerous cladding still need to be fixed.

The new rules, known as PAS9980, grade the fire risk posed by a tower block's cladding system into four categories: high, medium, tolerable, and low.

Only those assessed as high or medium risk will require the cladding to be removed, but all categories permit the cladding to be flammable.

Cladding campaigners say this relies too much on the judgement of fire safety assessors, who are not independently appointed and often employed by the building's freeholder or developer.

The government declined to be interviewed about the changes.

But the Ministry of Housing said in a statement it would speed up the process of removing cladding, providing a more proportionate, clear and consistent approach to a complex issue.

It said repaired buildings would be audited to make sure the work had been carried out properly.

Residents still in hotels a week after tower fire

Major fires still a risk under 'spineless' new safety law, construction boss warns

More buildings to receive dangerous cladding removal funding

But cladding campaigners believe a better approach would be to make sure all fire safety defects in tower blocks were addressed, not just cladding on exterior walls.

Ed Daffarn, who was the first person to warn about the dangers posed by cladding being added to Grenfell, watched the tower burn on the night of the fire.

He said he cannot believe, nearly ten years after the fire, that government officials, the fire safety industry and developers are still wrestling with the definition of what is safe.

"It shows the indifference and incompetence of the two different colours of government we've had in the last ten years," he says.

Daffarn said the building industry should also be made to fix fire safety defects in the buildings beyond the cladding if they're found to have not met the building regulation at the time of construction - a consideration removed from the new rules.

This approach is also supported by the insurance industry, and the Association of British Insurers says all flammable cladding should be removed.

When Natasha and other residents at her block were told a fire risk assessment showed the cladding needed to be removed, she says her buildings insurance went up by 94%.

As the flat is leasehold, the premium is included in her maintenance charges, which are now nearly £8,000 a year.

She and other residents are concerned that if her building is not fully fixed, and insurance premiums remain high if all the fire and safety risks not are addressed, it could remain unmortgageable and unsellable.

"I feel like I've been punished for getting onto the housing ladder so early," she says.

"It should be you buy a home, it's a safe place to be, no-one should have to be compromised or deciding whether they might live or not based on the home they buy."

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday claimed that several MLAs from the ruling BJP-led alliance in Uttar Pradesh are in contact
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Wednesday claimed that several MLAs from the ruling BJP-led alliance in Uttar Pradesh are in contact with his party ahead of the Rajya Sabha elections, while saying the SP would not make commitments it could not honour.“There are many who are in contact. But how do we adjust them? We do not want to make a promise and then go back on it,” Yadav said at a press conference at the SP office.The remarks came as the SP formally entered the Rajya Sabha contest in Uttar Pradesh, with party candidates Professor Ram Gopal Yadav and Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani filing their nomination papers. Akhilesh Yadav accompanied both candidates during the filing.SP sticks to alliance, winnability formulaAsked about the party's plans for next year's Uttar Pradesh Assembly polls, Yadav said the alliance that existed earlier would continue. On seat-sharing, he reiterated that the SP would use winnability as the basis for deciding which party contests a seat.“The SP has said this earlier and I am saying it again -- winnability is the basis for a seat,” he said.The Election Commission has announced that polling for 11 Rajya Sabha seats, 10 from Uttar Pradesh and one from Uttarakhand, will be held on October 16. The terms of the sitting members from the two states are due to expire on November 25.Rajya Sabha contest heats upYadav said the democratic system requires representatives to be elected by the people and lawmakers to subsequently elect members of the Upper House.“Democracy should not have dishonesty. Had the BJP not indulged in dishonesty, the SP would have had three Rajya Sabha MPs,” he said, referring to the previous Rajya Sabha election in which SP candidate Alok Ranjan lost after cross-voting.Yadav said the SP was now urging MLAs to use the opportunity to “wash away the past”.Uttar Pradesh deputy chief minister Keshav Prasad Maurya, however, claimed that 25 SP MLAs were in touch with the BJP.“We will surprise them. 25 of their MLAs are in touch with us,” Maurya said, according to news agency ANI.His remarks came after the SP announced Ram Gopal Yadav and Nathwani as its two candidates.Uttar Pradesh minister and Suheldev Bharatiya Samaj Party chief Om Prakash Rajbhar also questioned whether the SP's candidates reflected its PDA — Pichhada, Dalit and Alpashankhyak — formulation.He cautioned the party against attempting to secure a third seat at the risk of losing its second.Yadav defends Nathwani candidatureDefending the nomination of industrialist Dhanraj Parimal Nathwani, Yadav said he was pleased that the SP had the opportunity to send a representative of the younger generation and a “new way of thinking” to the Rajya Sabha.“The SP has decided to connect with the industrial sector and therefore, to make someone associated with the industry its Rajya Sabha member,” he said.Responding to criticism over backing an industrialist, Yadav said, “I think you should read about socialism again. I will give you a book by (Ram Manohar) Lohia.”He said socialist thought also focused on prosperity and equality and argued that governments across the country seek investment to drive economic growth.Yadav said the SP wanted to promote industries and employment in Uttar Pradesh, adding that the party would support those who contribute to economic growth, farmer employment and jobs for young people.Sugarcane payments and Raebareli remarksYadav also promised that sugarcane growers would receive pending payments within 24 to 48 hours if the SP formed the government in Uttar Pradesh. He said the party's election manifesto would include several measures for farmers.On his recent visit to Raebareli and allegations of police misconduct involving SP MLA Rahul Lodhi, Yadav questioned how police could behave in such a manner with an elected representative.“How can police behave like this with an elected representative?” he asked.He also said, “This time, it will be Lodhi versus (Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister) Yogi (Adityanath).”Yadav further said Uttar Pradesh's proposed target of becoming a USD 1-trillion economy could not be achieved through corruption, saying, “A USD-1-trillion economy will not be built through theft of offerings.”He also said the SP would continue to focus on farmers, recalling former prime minister Chaudhary Charan Singh and farmer leader Mahendra Singh Tikait.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Just over a quarter of nurdles cleared after River Tyne spillage
articles.summary: Scientists predict that nurdles will continue to wash up on North East beaches.
articles.body:
Only 28% of nurdles which spilled into a river have been recovered and are expected to continue washing up on beaches in the future, scientists have calculated.

Almost 18 tonnes of plastic nurdles are estimated to have spilled into the River Tyne after a collision between ships at the Port of Tyne in July.

However, only 5.14 tonnes have been recovered despite volunteers spending thousands of hours clearing beaches across the region, work by Newcastle University and the Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (Cefas) found.

South Tyneside Council's director of community operations Gary Kirsop, said the multi-agency group in charge of the nurdle response "remained committed".

The university and Cefas said nurdles were "likely to have dispersed beyond the Tyne estuary out into the North Sea".

The work, undertaken by the university, also said some nurdles "may remain within the river system" and will continue to wash up on parts of the coastline in future, depending on weather conditions, winds and tides.

North East mayor Kim McGuinness said this was upsetting for those caring for the region's coastline.

She has commissioned an independent review into the response and recovery, and said she is backing calls for a change in international rules about how plastic nurdles are transported.

McGuinness said: "It's vital the agencies involved in the clean up are ready and act quickly to continue their work when this happens."

Scientific and Techincal Advice Cell (STAC) has reviewed Cefas' modelling alongside recovery data and shoreline surveys.

It said modelling cannot accurately predict exactly when and where nurdles will wash up and the complete recovery of every nurdle was not considered achievable.

Dr Robert Bradburne, STAC chair, said: "As with any environmental incident of this nature, ongoing monitoring remains important and the situation should continue to be reviewed as further evidence becomes available."

articles.title: 8.86acre Bargain land case: PMLA court frames charges against Jharkhand CM Hemant Soren
articles.summary: RANCHI: A special PMLA court in Ranchi on Wednesday framed charges against Jharkhand chief minister Hemant Soren in the alleged 8.86-acre Bargain land
articles.body: RANCHI: A special PMLA court in Ranchi on Wednesday framed charges against Jharkhand chief minister Hemant Soren in the alleged 8.86-acre Bargain land fraud case, paving the way for the trial to begin, his lawyer said.“The special PMLA (Prevention of Money Laundering Act) court framed charges against the Jharkhand chief minister and now put the matter for trial,” Soren’s lawyer Sanjeev Sahay said.Soren appeared before the court through video conferencing. The trial will now proceed with the examination of witnesses, news agency PTI reported.The Enforcement Directorate had registered a money laundering case in connection with the alleged illegal acquisition and transfer of the land in Ranchi’s Bargain area.The case centres on allegations that Soren abused his position as chief minister to unlawfully acquire the land.The ED had alleged that forged official records were used to alter ownership details and that fake sellers and purchasers were involved in the transactions.The agency had also claimed that witnesses examined during its investigation confirmed Soren’s alleged involvement.Soren was arrested by the ED in January 2024 in connection with the land case and was granted bail by the Jharkhand High Court in June 2024.The high court, while granting bail, held that prima facie he was not guilty of the offence and that there was no likelihood of him committing an offence while on bail.The charge-framing proceedings had been deferred on September 24 after Soren’s counsel sought time to examine a list of unverified documents supplied by the ED.The PMLA court subsequently fixed September 30 for the proceedings.The court had already framed charges against several other accused in the case, all of whom pleaded not guilty.(With agency inputs)Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news.
